summary: This work introduces directional tile codes, a family of quantum low-density parity-check codes compatible with planar nearest-neighbour superconducting qubit architectures, where syndrome extraction uses only iSWAP-based walks on a 2D square grid. The codes achieve circuit-level logical error rates up to 1000× lower than rotated surface codes at comparable footprints (~30 qubits per logical qubit), combining high code efficiency with strictly local connectivity.
motivation: High-performance qLDPC codes promise overhead reduction for fault-tolerant quantum computation but typically require long-range connectivity or qubit shuttling, which are difficult to implement in superconducting processors constrained to planar nearest-neighbour gates. The work addresses whether substantial finite-size advantages over surface codes can be retained under strict 2D locality constraints.
method: Directional tile codes use directional words—ordered strings of lattice steps—to simultaneously define stabiliser supports and specify the measurement schedule. Nearest-neighbour iSWAP walks dynamically generate check-data interactions during syndrome extraction, where CXSWAP gates both accumulate syndrome parity and route quantum information through the lattice. Stabiliser measurement achieves optimal constant depth $w+2$ independent of code size, where $w$ is the word weight.
result: Finite-size instances such as $[[323,14,15]]$ codes achieve code-efficiency ratios nearly an order of magnitude larger than rotated surface-code patches; circuit-level simulations at $p=0.001$ show per-logical per-round logical error rates of $p_L \sim 10^{-7}$ versus $\sim 10^{-5}$ for surface codes at comparable footprints, representing up to 1000× improvement with circuit-efficiency ratio $\eta_\mathrm{circ} \gtrsim 5$.
